\chapter{The First Verbs}
\label{ch:first-verbs}
\hlchaptermodality{5}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can build short present-tense French sentences with the chapter's first verbs.}

Until now you have assembled fixed phrases. This chapter hands you a pattern instead: the regular -er verbs, the largest verb family in French by a wide margin. Learn the one template and thousands of verbs come with it — and with it you build your first sentence that nobody handed you pre-made.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[parler]{parler — \textquotedblleft{}to speak,\textquotedblright{} and the great regular French verb}

\label{lesson:FR-C05-parler}



\begin{quote}
Until now you've assembled fixed phrases. \textbf{parler} (\textquotedblleft{}to speak\textquotedblright{}) is your first real \textbf{verb} — and it's the model for the \textbf{biggest} French verb family by far: the \textbf{-er} verbs. Learn this one pattern and you can drive thousands.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{er-ending} — the infinitive \textbf{-er} is a clean \emph{ay}: \textbf{parler} = \emph{par-LAY} (the \emph{r} is silent in the ending). The stem is \emph{parl-}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{parler} comes from Late Latin \textbf{parabolāre}, \emph{\textquotedblleft{}to tell parables, to discourse\textquotedblright{}} — from \textbf{parabola}, \textquotedblleft{}a comparison, a speech\textquotedblright{} (itself from Greek \emph{parabolē}, \textquotedblleft{}a throwing-beside\textquotedblright{}). So to \emph{speak}, in French, is at root to \emph{tell parables}. That root fans into English:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{parable} — the story-comparison itself.
  \item \textbf{parole} — a spoken word of honour (a prisoner's \emph{parole}).
  \item \textbf{palaver} — a long talk; \textbf{parley} — to talk terms; even \textbf{parliament} — a \emph{talking}-place.
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the -er present tense (and its silent trap)}]
Drop \textbf{-er}, add the ending for the person:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{ending} & \textbf{\emph{parler} $\to$} & \textbf{sounds like} \\
\midrule
je & \textbf{-e} & \textbf{je parle} & \emph{parl} \\
tu & \textbf{-es} & \textbf{tu parles} & \emph{parl} \\
il / elle & \textbf{-e} & \textbf{il parle} & \emph{parl} \\
nous & -ons & \textbf{nous parlons} & par-LON \\
vous & -ez & \textbf{vous parlez} & par-LAY \\
ils / elles & \textbf{-ent} & \textbf{ils parlent} & \emph{parl} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Here is the great French surprise: \textbf{-e, -es, and -ent are all SILENT} — \emph{je parle}, \emph{tu parles}, \emph{ils parlent} \textbf{all sound identical}, just \emph{parl}. Only \emph{nous} (\emph{-ons}) and \emph{vous} (\emph{-ez}) are audible.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: why French keeps its pronouns}]
That silence has a consequence which shapes the whole language. In Spanish the ending alone tells you who is speaking — \emph{hablo} (\textquotedblleft{}I speak\textquotedblright{}) against \emph{hablas} (\textquotedblleft{}you speak\textquotedblright{}) — so the pronoun can be dropped. In French your ear cannot hear any difference between \emph{parle}, \emph{parles} and \emph{parlent}, so the \textbf{pronoun must stay} to carry the person. \emph{Je} and \emph{tu} are not optional decoration in French; they are the only thing telling you who is doing the speaking.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}parler\textquotedblright{} — \emph{par-LAY}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}je parle, tu parles, il parle\textquotedblright{} — all \emph{parl}, identical
  \item \textquotedblleft{}parler\textquotedblright{} then English \textquotedblleft{}parable, parole, palaver\textquotedblright{} — the \emph{parabola} root
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Latin word is \emph{parler} from, and its English cousins? (\emph{parabolāre} $\leftarrow$ \emph{parabola} — parable, parole.) Which three present-tense endings are silent? (\emph{-e, -es, -ent} — je/tu/ils all sound \emph{parl}.) Why does French keep \emph{je/tu} when Spanish drops \emph{yo/tú}? (The endings are silent, so the pronoun carries the person.) Next: \textbf{habiter}, \textquotedblleft{}to live.\textquotedblright{}
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[habiter]{habiter — \textquotedblleft{}to live,\textquotedblright{} and it's about \emph{having a place}}

\label{lesson:FR-C05-habiter}



\begin{quote}
A second \textbf{-er} verb — snap it into the exact template you just learned. \textbf{habiter} (\textquotedblleft{}to live, to dwell\textquotedblright{}) lets you say \emph{where} you live, the answer to a \emph{où} (\textquotedblleft{}where\textquotedblright{}) question.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{silent-final} — the \textbf{h is silent} (French \emph{h} never sounds): \textbf{habiter} = \emph{a-bee-TAY}. Same \emph{-er} = \emph{ay} ending as \emph{parler}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{habiter} comes from Latin \textbf{habitāre}, \emph{\textquotedblleft{}to dwell, to keep on having {[}a place{]}\textquotedblright{}} — the \textbf{frequentative} of \textbf{habēre}, \textquotedblleft{}to have.\textquotedblright{} To \emph{dwell} somewhere is to \emph{keep having} it as your place. That root is thoroughly English:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{habitat} — the place a creature dwells.
  \item \textbf{inhabit}, \textbf{inhabitant}, \textbf{habitation} — to dwell in / one who dwells.
  \item and (via \emph{habēre}, \textquotedblleft{}have\textquotedblright{}) \textbf{habit} — what you \textquotedblleft{}keep having,\textquotedblright{} and \textbf{able}, \textbf{ability} (what you \textquotedblleft{}have\textquotedblright{} it in you to do).
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: same -er template}]
Drop \textbf{-er}, add the endings — identical to \emph{parler}, silent trap and all:

| j'habite · tu habites · il habite | (all \emph{a-BEET}) |

| nous habitons · vous habitez | (a-bee-TON · a-bee-TAY) |

Note \textbf{j'habite} — \emph{je} elides to \textbf{j'} before the vowel of \emph{habite} (the \emph{h} is silent, so it counts as a vowel). Now you can answer \emph{où} questions:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{J'habite à Paris.} — \textquotedblleft{}I live in Paris.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}habiter\textquotedblright{} — \emph{a-bee-TAY}, silent \emph{h}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}j'habite, tu habites, il habite\textquotedblright{} — all \emph{a-BEET}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}habiter\textquotedblright{} then English \textquotedblleft{}habitat, inhabit\textquotedblright{} — the \emph{habitāre} root
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Latin verb is \emph{habiter} from, and what does it literally involve? (\emph{habitāre}, \textquotedblleft{}keep having a place\textquotedblright{} — from \emph{habēre}, \textquotedblleft{}to have.\textquotedblright{}) English cousins? (Habitat, inhabit, habitation.) Say \textquotedblleft{}I live in Paris.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{J'habite à Paris.}) Next: \textbf{travailler}, \textquotedblleft{}to work.\textquotedblright{}
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[travailler]{travailler — \textquotedblleft{}to work,\textquotedblright{} and the torture behind \textquotedblleft{}travel\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:FR-C05-travailler}



\begin{quote}
A third \textbf{-er} verb, and it shares its dark, delightful origin with a Spanish word you may already know: \textbf{travailler} (\textquotedblleft{}to work\textquotedblright{}) began as a word for \textbf{torture}, and it's the secret ancestor of English \textbf{travel}.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{ai-y} — the \textbf{-ill-} is a \emph{y} glide: \textbf{travailler} = \emph{tra-va-YAY}. Same \emph{-er} = \emph{ay} ending.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{travailler} comes from Vulgar Latin \textbf{tripaliāre}, \emph{\textquotedblleft{}to torture\textquotedblright{}} — from \textbf{tripalium}, a Roman instrument of torture made of \textbf{three stakes} (\emph{tri-} \textquotedblleft{}three\textquotedblright{} + \emph{pālus} \textquotedblleft{}stake\textquotedblright{} $\to$ English \emph{pale}, \emph{impale}).

The slide of meaning is grim and logical: \emph{torture} $\to$ \emph{painful toil} $\to$ \textbf{work}. And two English words came down the same road:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{travail} — painful, laborious effort.
  \item \textbf{travel} — journeying was once such an \textbf{ordeal} that \emph{travail} (toil) became \emph{travel} (to make a journey). You are, etymologically, \emph{tortured} every time you travel.
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Spanish \textbf{trabajar} (\textquotedblleft{}to work\textquotedblright{}) comes from the very same \emph{tripaliāre} — a perfect cross-language twin, torture and all. The middle of the word went one way in each language: the \emph{-al-} stayed in French (\emph{travail}, \emph{travailler}) and softened to \emph{-aj-} in Spanish (\emph{trabajo}, \emph{trabajar}).
\end{culture}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: same -er template}]
| je travaille · tu travailles · il travaille | (all \emph{tra-VYE}) |

| nous travaillons · vous travaillez |  |

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Je travaille à Paris.} — \textquotedblleft{}I work in Paris.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Nothing new to learn — that's the point. \textbf{One template, every -er verb.}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}travailler\textquotedblright{} — \emph{tra-va-YAY}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}je travaille\textquotedblright{} — \emph{je tra-VYE}, \textquotedblleft{}I work\textquotedblright{}
  \item travailler $\to$ travail $\to$ travel — torture became a journey; twin of Spanish \emph{trabajar}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{travailler} originally mean, and from what device? (\textquotedblleft{}To torture,\textquotedblright{} $\leftarrow$ \emph{tripalium}, three stakes.) What two English words share the root? (\emph{Travail} and \emph{travel}.) Its Spanish twin? (\emph{Trabajar} — same \emph{tripaliāre}.) Next: build your first full sentence — \textbf{Je parle français}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Je parle français]{Je parle français — your first real sentence}

\label{lesson:FR-C05-je-parle-francais}



\begin{quote}
The moment it all pays off: you take a \textbf{verb} you conjugated and a \textbf{noun}, and build a sentence \textbf{no one handed you pre-made} — \emph{Je parle français}, \textquotedblleft{}I speak French.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{soft-c-s} — \textbf{français} = \emph{frahn-SEH}. The cedilla under the \textbf{ç} forces a soft \emph{s} where a plain \emph{c} would have been hard.
  \item The opening \emph{fran-} is nasal, and the final \emph{-ais} is a plain \emph{eh}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{français} = \textquotedblleft{}French\textquotedblright{} — both the language and a French person — from \textbf{Francia}, \textquotedblleft{}land of the \textbf{Franks}\textquotedblright{}: the Germanic people who settled Roman Gaul and gave France its name. And here is the twist: the Franks' own name meant \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}free.\textquotedblright{}} That is why English \textbf{frank} and \textbf{frankly} mean open and unguarded, and why the old French coin was called a \emph{franc}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two rules hiding in four words}]
Snap together two things you own:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Je} (I, $\leftarrow$ \emph{ego}) + \textbf{parle} (speak, from \emph{parler}) = \textbf{Je parle français.}
\end{quote}

A complete, grammatical French sentence. Two rules are hiding in it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{You keep the \emph{je}.} Spanish drops its pronoun — \emph{hablo español} says \textquotedblleft{}I speak Spanish\textquotedblright{} with no word for \textquotedblleft{}I,\textquotedblright{} because the ending \emph{-o} carries the person. French cannot do that: \emph{parle}, \emph{parles} and \emph{parlent} all sound alike, so \textbf{the pronoun must stay}. This is the single biggest structural difference between French and its Iberian cousins.
  \item \textbf{No article on the language} here: \emph{je parle français}, not \emph{je parle le français}.
\end{itemize}

Swap the pieces and it generates:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{J'habite à Paris.} — \textquotedblleft{}I live in Paris.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{Tu parles français ?} — \textquotedblleft{}Do you speak French?\textquotedblright{} (just raise the tone).
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Je parle français\textquotedblright{} — \emph{zhuh parl frahn-SEH}
  \item keep the \emph{je} — French can't drop it (unlike Spanish \emph{hablo})
  \item swap — \textquotedblleft{}Tu parles français ?\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}J'habite à Paris\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does \emph{français} come from, and what did the Franks' name mean? (\emph{Francia}, \textquotedblleft{}land of the Franks\textquotedblright{}; the name meant \textquotedblleft{}free\textquotedblright{} — English \emph{frank}.) Why must French keep \emph{je} where Spanish drops \emph{yo}? (French endings are silent, so the pronoun carries the person.) Next: practice.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — making sentences with -er verbs}

\label{lesson:FR-C05-practice}



\begin{quote}
For the first time you're not reciting phrases — you're \textbf{building} sentences from a pattern. Drill the three verbs, and burn in the French rule the whole language turns on: \textbf{keep the pronoun} (the endings are silent).
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn: conjugate on command}
Run each through \emph{je / tu / il}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{parler}: je parle · tu parles · il parle — all \textbf{parl}
  \item \textbf{habiter}: j'habite · tu habites · il habite — all \textbf{a-beet}
  \item \textbf{travailler}: je travaille · tu travailles · il travaille — all \textbf{tra-vye}
\end{itemize}

Every singular form (and the \emph{ils} form) \textbf{sounds the same} — the \emph{-e/-es/-ent} are silent. That's why \emph{je, tu, il} stay put: they carry the person your ear can't hear.

\subsection*{Your turn: say something real}
\begin{quote}
— \textbf{Tu parles} français ? — Oui, je \textbf{parle} un peu. (Do you speak French? — Yes, I speak a little.) — \textbf{Où} habites-tu ? — \textbf{J'habite} à Lyon. Et je \textbf{travaille} à Paris. — Merci ! — De rien.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built this chapter}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{the regular -er present tense} — drop \emph{-er}, add \emph{-e/-es/-e/-ons/-ez/-ent}; the singular + \emph{ils} endings are \textbf{silent}, so the pronoun is mandatory (the big contrast with Spanish/Italian pro-drop).
  \item \textbf{parler} ($\leftarrow$ \emph{parabolāre} $\to$ parable/parole), \textbf{habiter} ($\leftarrow$ \emph{habitāre} $\to$ habitat/inhabit), \textbf{travailler} ($\leftarrow$ \emph{tripalium} $\to$ travail/travel; twin of Spanish \emph{trabajar}).
  \item \textbf{Je parle français} — your first self-assembled sentence (\emph{français} $\leftarrow$ \emph{Francia}, the Franks = \textquotedblleft{}free\textquotedblright{}).
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item conjugate all three verbs, je/tu/il — hear that they don't change
  \item answer about yourself — where you live, where you work, what you speak
  \item chain it — \textquotedblleft{}Bonjour ! Je parle français. Tu parles français ? … Au revoir !\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Tu parles français ? — Oui, je parle un peu.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which -er endings are silent, and what follows from that? (\emph{-e, -es, -ent} — so French keeps its subject pronouns.) Give \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} forms of the three verbs. (\emph{Je parle, j'habite, je travaille}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}I live in Paris and I work in Lyon.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{J'habite à Paris et je travaille à Lyon.}) French now moves in real sentences.
\end{tcolorbox}
